blocks.content: A system that hands out and reclaims memory all day long does not usually run out of memory in the way people first imagine. It rarely reaches a point where every byte is genuinely in use. Instead, it reaches a point where plenty of memory is technically free, yet a new request still fails, because that free memory has been left behind in pieces that do not fit together the way the request needs.

This chapter is about that exact failure mode, called fragmentation. We will look at the two distinct forms it takes, external fragmentation and internal fragmentation, work through a full concrete example of each so the difference is unmistakable, compare them directly side by side, trace each one back to the allocation strategy that causes it, and cover compaction, the classic fix for external fragmentation, including its real and often underestimated cost.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864476-614219102.png
1. The General Problem: How Free Memory Gets Wasted
blocks.text: 1. The General Problem: How Free Memory Gets Wasted

blocks.content: Picture a system that has been running for hours. Processes have started, requested memory, run for a while, and exited, over and over. Each time a process is loaded it claims a chunk of memory, and each time a process exits that chunk is handed back as free. Because processes are different sizes and start and stop at different times, no two of these allocate and free cycles ever line up neatly with the ones before them.

After enough of these cycles, the free memory in the system is no longer one clean, usable region. It is broken up, or fragmented, into many separate pieces of different sizes sitting in different places. The memory has not actually disappeared, if you add up every free byte the total can look perfectly healthy, but the arrangement of that free memory is what actually determines whether a new request can be satisfied, and the arrangement is exactly what a simple free memory counter hides from you.
Fragmentation is not about how much memory is free. It is about whether that free memory is arranged in a way that can actually satisfy the next request.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: Fragmentation is what happens when free memory exists in enough total quantity to satisfy a request, but the way it is arranged, or the way it was carved up, makes it impossible to actually hand that memory to the request.
Two ways memory gets wasted

There are exactly two distinct patterns this waste falls into, and operating systems textbooks name them precisely so they are never confused with one another. Both waste real memory, but they waste it in opposite places relative to an allocation, and the rest of this chapter treats each one on its own terms before putting them side by side.

["External fragmentation: wasted space that sits between allocations, scattered around as small leftover holes in the free list.","Internal fragmentation: wasted space that sits within a single allocation, hidden inside a block that already looks fully used from the outside."]
items: External fragmentation: wasted space that sits between allocations, scattered around as small leftover holes in the free list.
Internal fragmentation: wasted space that sits within a single allocation, hidden inside a block that already looks fully used from the outside.

blocks.content: 2. External Fragmentation

External fragmentation shows up in systems that use variable sized, contiguous allocation, meaning every allocated block occupies one unbroken stretch of memory sized to exactly what was requested. The problem appears when free memory does exist in enough total quantity to satisfy a new request, but it is scattered across many small, non contiguous blocks instead of gathered into one block large enough. Even though enough free memory technically exists somewhere in the system, the request cannot actually be satisfied, because no single free block reaches the size it needs.

This pattern accumulates naturally over time rather than appearing all at once. As processes of different sizes are loaded and later exit at different moments, each one leaves behind a hole shaped exactly like itself, sitting wherever that process happened to be. There is no guarantee that two of these holes will ever end up next to each other, so instead of merging into something bigger they simply pile up as a scattering of small, unrelated gaps between the blocks that are still in use.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864476-506459256.png
A worked example

Suppose five processes, A through E, are currently loaded in memory, with small free holes left behind between them wherever an earlier process has already exited. The holes measure 4KB, 3KB, 5KB, 2KB, and 6KB. Now a new process arrives asking for a single contiguous block of 20KB.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864476-545389127.png

{"headers":["Free Hole","Size"],"rows":[["Hole 1","4KB"],["Hole 2","3KB"],["Hole 3","5KB"],["Hole 4","2KB"],["Hole 5","6KB"],["Total free","20KB"],["Largest single hole","6KB"],["Request","20KB, fails"]]}

Add up the five holes and the total is exactly 20KB, precisely enough to satisfy the request on paper. But the allocator cannot hand out five separate holes glued together, it can only hand out one contiguous block, and the largest single hole available is only 6KB. The request fails, not because memory ran out, but because the memory that remained free was never arranged in a way this request could use.

blocks.title: The number that actually matters
blocks.content: When judging whether a contiguous request can succeed, the sum of all free holes is close to irrelevant. What matters is the size of the single largest contiguous hole. A system can report gigabytes of free memory and still reject a modest request if that free memory is split into pieces smaller than the request itself.
3. Internal Fragmentation

Internal fragmentation looks like the opposite problem, and it comes from an opposite kind of allocation scheme. Instead of allocating variable sized contiguous blocks, the system allocates memory in fixed size chunks, all identical, all one constant size decided in advance. A process asking for slightly more than one chunk boundary cannot be given a partial chunk, so its request is rounded up to the next full chunk, and the space inside that chunk beyond what the process actually needed goes to waste.

The defining feature of internal fragmentation is exactly where that wasted space lives. It sits inside a block that has already been handed out to a specific process, not out in the open free list. Paging is the textbook example of a scheme built entirely on fixed size chunks, and because a process memory need is almost never an exact multiple of the page size, some amount of internal fragmentation in the final page of a process is essentially guaranteed. Averaged across many processes, this typically works out to about half a page of waste per process, a cost that is small individually but adds up across an entire system.
A worked example

Suppose the system only ever hands out memory in fixed 20KB chunks, and a process asks for 18KB. There is no way to give it a partial chunk, so it receives one full 20KB block. Of that block, 18KB is genuinely used, and 2KB sits idle, unused, for as long as that process holds the block.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864948-555049243.png

blocks.title: Sealed inside, not reusable
blocks.content: That 2KB is not sitting in a free list waiting for somebody else to claim it. It belongs entirely to this one process, counted as allocated even though it is empty, and no other process can ever be given it while this allocation stands. This is precisely what makes internal fragmentation invisible to the allocator, from its point of view the whole 20KB block is simply in use.

Placing the two patterns next to each other makes the distinction impossible to miss. In external fragmentation, the wasted space is the green free blocks sitting between the blue used blocks, still nominally available to anyone, if only a request small enough came along. In internal fragmentation, the wasted space is the red region sitting fully inside a single blue block, already handed out, permanently unavailable to any other process.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864948-461584503.png
4. Internal vs External Fragmentation, Side by Side
blocks.text: 4. Internal vs External Fragmentation, Side by Side

blocks.content: With a full worked example of each behind us, the comparison can now be stated plainly and precisely, in a form worth memorizing exactly as written, since this distinction is one of the most commonly tested ideas in memory management.

{"headers":["Aspect","External Fragmentation","Internal Fragmentation"],"rows":[["Where the waste lives","Between allocations, scattered around memory as separate free holes","Within a single allocation, hidden inside a block that is already handed out"],["Visible in the free list?","Yes, it shows up as many small free blocks","No, the allocator sees the block as fully in use"],["Caused by","Variable sized, contiguous memory allocation","Fixed size allocation chunks"],["Grows worse from","Repeated allocate and free cycles over time","A request size that does not divide evenly into the fixed unit"]]}

One more way to hold onto the distinction: external fragmentation is a problem about the space between things, while internal fragmentation is a problem about the space inside one thing. Once that single sentence is internalized, the rest of the terminology tends to fall into place on its own.
5. Why Each Pattern Emerges: The Allocation Strategy Is the Root Cause
blocks.text: 5. Why Each Pattern Emerges: The Allocation Strategy Is the Root Cause

blocks.content: External fragmentation is not a rare accident that only shows up under unusual conditions, it is the near guaranteed result of any allocation strategy that hands out variable sized, contiguous blocks. First Fit, Best Fit, and Worst Fit are the three classic strategies for choosing which free hole to use for an incoming request, and every one of them is placing a variable sized request into a variable sized hole, which almost always leaves an odd sized remainder behind.

First Fit scans the free list from the start and grabs the first hole big enough, which is fast but tends to leave small unusable slivers early in memory. Best Fit searches every hole and picks the smallest one that still satisfies the request, which minimizes waste for that one allocation but often carves out tiny leftover slivers too small for almost anything else. Worst Fit deliberately grabs the largest hole available, hoping the leftover stays big enough to be useful, but in practice that one large hole simply keeps shrinking a little with every allocation that draws from it.

{"headers":["Strategy","How It Chooses","Typical Result"],"rows":[["First Fit","The first hole encountered that is large enough","Fast, but leaves scattered small slivers, especially early in memory"],["Best Fit","The smallest hole that still fits the request","Minimizes waste for one allocation, but tends to leave many tiny, unusable slivers"],["Worst Fit","The largest hole currently available","Keeps one big region usable for longer, but that region keeps eroding with each allocation"]]}
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864949-359934406.png
blocks.alt: Why Each Pattern Emerges: The Allocation Strategy Is the Root Cause

blocks.content: Internal fragmentation, by contrast, is the near guaranteed result of fixed size allocation schemes. Paging is the clearest example, physical memory is carved into fixed size frames and every process is allocated in equally fixed size pages, so the allocator can never hand out anything smaller than a whole page. Any process whose actual memory need is not an exact multiple of the page size wastes part of its final page, every single time, simply because there is no finer unit available to give it.
6. Compaction: The Classic Fix for External Fragmentation
blocks.text: 6. Compaction: The Classic Fix for External Fragmentation

blocks.content: Compaction is the classic response to external fragmentation. The idea is direct: physically shift the allocated blocks in memory so they sit immediately adjacent to one another with no gaps between them, which pushes every scrap of free space out of the middle and consolidates it into one single large contiguous region at one end of memory. A request that none of the original scattered holes could satisfy alone can now be granted from that one merged region.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864949-258345176.png
blocks.alt: Compaction: The Classic Fix for External Fragmentation

blocks.content: It is important to be honest about what compaction actually costs, because it is easy to describe it as if it were a free cleanup step the operating system can run whenever convenient. In reality, compaction means physically copying the contents of every block that moves, byte by byte, from its old location to its new one, and then updating every reference, base register, or page table entry that pointed at the old location so it now points at the new one.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864949-796097140.png
blocks.alt: Compaction: The Classic Fix for External Fragmentation

blocks.content: That copying takes real time, and the time it takes is proportional to how much data has to move, not some small fixed constant. Compacting a system holding gigabytes of long lived allocations can be a genuinely slow, disruptive operation that may require pausing the processes whose memory is being relocated, not a quick piece of background housekeeping.
7. Paging: Eliminating External Fragmentation by Design
blocks.text: 7. Paging: Eliminating External Fragmentation by Design

blocks.content: Paging sidesteps external fragmentation almost entirely, and it does so structurally rather than through any cleanup step like compaction. Because paging allocates memory in small, fixed size pages rather than variable sized contiguous blocks, satisfying a request for more memory just means finding enough free frames anywhere in physical memory. Every frame is exactly the same size and fully interchangeable, and a process pages do not need to sit next to each other at all, so there is never a need to search for one large contiguous hole in the first place.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408864949-462923050.png
blocks.alt: Paging: Eliminating External Fragmentation by Design

blocks.content: This is a genuine structural fix rather than a workaround, but it is not a free win. Paging trades external fragmentation away almost entirely and gets internal fragmentation in return, since every process still rounds its memory need up to a whole number of fixed size pages. It is a trade, not an elimination of waste altogether, just a change in which kind of waste the system has to live with.
8. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

The single most frequent error with this topic is mixing up which kind of fragmentation is which, describing scattered holes between blocks as internal, or describing wasted space inside one block as external. A reliable way to keep it straight: internal fragmentation is waste inside one allocation, exactly as the word internal suggests, while external fragmentation is waste outside allocations, sitting in the open free list between them.

A second common mistake is treating compaction as though it were essentially free or instantaneous, something the operating system can simply trigger in the background at no real cost. As covered above, compaction means physically copying memory and fixing up every reference to it, and that work takes real, sometimes significant, time proportional to how much data has to move. Presenting compaction as a free lunch is a frequent and avoidable gap in an otherwise solid answer.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to give one crisp, concrete example of each type on the spot, distinctly, rather than a vague dictionary definition. For external fragmentation, describe scattered holes that add up to enough total space but with none large enough alone, the 20KB example from this chapter works well. For internal fragmentation, describe a fixed size allocation, such as a 20KB or 4KB chunk, holding a smaller amount of actual data, with the remainder wasted inside that same chunk. Naming the specific allocation strategy behind each, First Fit, Best Fit, or Worst Fit for external, paging for internal, ties the whole answer together and shows real understanding rather than a memorized definition.
